newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Clyde, Gulf Canada renew mudslinging.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Clyde, Gulf Canada renew mudslinging.

text.p: Bid target Clyde Petroleum Plc and its predator Gulf Canada Resources Ltd entered a new round of mudslinging on Tuesday as the bid battle over the British oil exploration and production firm hotted up.
In a document to Clyde shareholders, Gulf Canada accused Clyde's management from making empty promises, while adding that the company had poor development prospects.
"Clyde shareholders have a choice: the certainty of 105 pence in cash today against the empty promises of Clyde's directors," said J.P Bryan, president and chief executive of Gulf Canada.
Gulf Canada's offer values clyde at 432 million pounds ($717.5 million).
Clyde quickly reacted by saying Gulf Canada issued predictable, misleading and irrelevant rhetoric.
"The rhetoric is predictable, but shareholders should not be misled," Clyde's managing director Roy Franklin told Reuters.
He said Gulf Canada was selectively looking back to before 1993, just ahead of a strategy overhaul, to try to demonstrate Clyde was a poorly performing company.
"Harking back to the late eighties or early nineties and previous strategies is quite frankly irrelevant and misleading," Franklin said.
Gulf Canada's Bryan, meanwhile, said Clyde had a mature asset portfolio with declining reserves and reserve life with limited development opportunities and exploration prospects.
"Clyde's strategy...is highly unlikely to deliver any real growth in value to shareholders," he said.
Gulf Canada launched its hostile bid from Clyde on December 18 with Clyde having until January 28 to produce its final defence document.

Rather than Clyde growth prospects, Gulf Canada said it was interested in the British firm because of the location of its main assets -- the North Sea and offshore Australia, which were politically stable regions with favourable tax regimes.
Clyde's shares closed down 2-1/2 pence to 120-1/2 pence amid market hopes of a counterbid.
But Gulf Canada said it is unlikely the offer for Clyde will be trumped by a rival bidder.
Gulf chief financial officer Greg Glick told reporters any potential rival bidders would not been able to detect value not already appreciated in Gulf's offer.
"When other companies look at Clyde they are going to see the same thing as we did," Glick said during a press conference call.
He said the share price was driven well above Gulf's bid because of "arbitrage" and added he was confident the shares would come down shortly.
Gulf Canada was not disappointed that just 0.02 percent of Clyde's issued share capital had been tendered up until January 10. Glick said this kind of level was expected. ($1=.6021 Pound)
